question: The Commission recently published its long-delayed report on the application of the Term Extension Directive (Directive 2011/77/EU1), originally due in 2016. This directive extended copyright protection of music recordings from 50 to 70 years, despite no proven economic benefit, while performances in audiovisual recordings received no similar extension.

Thus, copyright protection varies depending on whether a performance is fixed in a sound or audiovisual recording, a discrimination not seen in authors’ copyright. Actors and other audiovisual performers have long sought to end this inequality.

Although the Commission’s report finds the economic impact on music recordings to be minimal, it advises against equalising protection for audiovisual performances because of a lack of proven benefit. This contradictory position upholds an unequal treatment of performers, based solely on the medium in which their performances are recorded. 1.

Why does the Commission look into the economic value of audiovisual recordings as a condition for extending the term of protection, when such evidence was not delivered prior to the granting of the extension of the term of protection for music recordings?

Can the Commission confirm that the Member States have the competence to remove this discrimination in national legislation and provide audiovisual performances with an equal term of protection to that of music recordings?
OJ L 265, 11.10.2011, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/77/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2026) The Commission analysed the possible need for an extension of the term of protection to audiovisual performers and also film producers in the Staff Working Document1 published in 2020.

In both the Staff Working Document and the later Commission Report2 on the application of the 2011 Term Directive,3 the Commission concluded that the available evidence did not call for such an extension. The 2020 Staff Working Document analysed the potential effects of a term extension on audiovisual performers and also film producers, as well as on content providers and on the availability of films.

It also pointed out the different contracting and collective management practices between the music and audiovisual sectors. The expected commercial lifespan of films was taken into consideration in assessing the expected impacts on the revenues of audiovisual performers. The commercial lifespan of films can be distinguished from the economic exploitation of sound recordings over time.

This was a factor in assessing the impact of the term extension on the revenue of music performers in the 2025 Report. The term of protection of performers is fully harmonised by Article 3 of Directive 2006/116, and save as is provided in Article 10, that Directive leaves open no possibility for Member States to introduce a different term of protection for any category of performers.
